response.text:
RSS originates in Petrov and Macdonald’s RecSys 2022 paper, *Effective and Efficient Training for Sequential Recommendation using Recency Sampling* (DOI: 10.1145/3523227.3546785), later expanded into the journal article prefixed “RSS:”. Crucially, RSS does **not** construct strictly truncated prefixes: it samples target positions, removes those items, and retains the remaining sequence—including interactions occurring after an interior target. Unlike BERT4Rec, it removes target positions rather than inserting mask tokens, and predicts a set of positives from the remaining history rather than reconstructing each masked position. Experiments use BCE and LambdaRank. [Original paper, §4 and Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.02643)

For positions k=0,…,n−1, RSS draws c=max(1,floor(nτ)) targets with replacement using p(k)∝α^(n−k). Thus the newest position has per-draw probability (1−α)/(1−α^n), the oldest α^(n−1)(1−α)/(1−α^n); inclusion probability is 1−(1−p(k))^c. These formulas follow directly from the paper’s sampling rule. α=1 gives uniform sampling; smaller α increasingly favors the endpoint. Recency acts through target selection, without requiring an explicit recency-weighted loss. [RSS equations and algorithm](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.02643)

BERT4Rec instead randomly selects a proportion ρ of positions, reconstructs their identities using both left and right context, and averages masked-target negative log-likelihood. Ordinary masking gives endpoints the same selection probability as other positions; additional last-item-only examples favor the endpoint, but the paper specifies no fixed mixing probability. Inference appends a mask. Originality assessment: recency-biased target selection already has a direct precedent in RSS; retaining positional masks and per-position bidirectional reconstruction distinguishes a BERT4Rec adaptation, but does not alone establish novelty. [BERT4Rec, §3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.06690)
